before.text: The process begins with the Data Acquisition phase.
Here, data is collected from the vehicle's onboard diagnostics port using a connected device.
This step captures trusted, normal in-vehicle network data.
These network traces represent the baseline behavior of the vehicle under normal operating conditions.
This clean baseline data is then passed to the model development phase.
In the Model Development phase, the core machine learning models are trained.
The training process utilizes the attack-free data along with specified model hyperparameters.
These inputs are used to configure and train two distinct components.
First, a Predictor model, featuring an encoder-decoder neural network architecture, is trained to reconstruct or predict normal network sequences.
Second, a Detector model is established to learn the boundary of normal behavior based on the predictor's performance.
Once trained, these models are deployed to the testing phase.
The Model Testing phase evaluates the system's ability to identify security threats.
During testing, new network data, which may contain attacks, is introduced.
This evaluation data is fed directly into the pipeline of trained models.
The trained models process the incoming data sequentially.
First, the predictor model processes the testing data to generate predictions.
The system then calculates the deviations between the actual network data and the model's predictions.
These deviations are passed to the detector model, which determines if they fall outside the normal boundary.
If the deviations are classified as anomalous, an alert is triggered.
Finally, the system outputs an anomaly alert to warn of a potential security breach.

examples.prompt: Animate the Cardinal 1 and Cardinal K boxes incrementally instead of together.

before.text: The ResNeSt block receives an input feature map with specified dimensions (h, w, c).
The input is distributed in parallel across Cardinal 1 to Cardinal K groups, where each group processes split convolution branches and aggregates them with Split Attention.
The representations from all cardinal groups are concatenated along the channel dimension.
A final 1x1 convolution projects the concatenated representations to match the target channel dimension.
Finally, the result is combined with the original input through a shortcut connection to produce the block output.

after.text: The ResNeSt block receives an input feature map with specified height, width, and channels.
The input is distributed across multiple cardinal groups, starting with the first cardinal group.
Within this group, the first split processes the features using a one-by-one convolution followed by a three-by-three convolution.
This transformation is replicated across all split branches within the cardinal group.
A Split Attention module then fuses the representations from each split to generate the cardinal group's output.
The same structure operates in parallel across the remaining cardinal groups.
In the final cardinal group, the first split applies its convolutional layers.
The subsequent splits perform identical feature transformations.
Split Attention then integrates the split feature representations.
The outputs from all cardinal groups are concatenated along the channel dimension.
A final one-by-one convolution projects the concatenated features to the target channel dimension.
Finally, the result is combined with the original input through a shortcut connection to form the block output.

examples.prompt: Represent the  whole Detection and  Attribution Layer module together in one shot. Only go into the details of the other two (”Physics Perception Layer” and “Reasoning & Diagnosis Layer”

before.text: The fault diagnosis and reasoning framework is structured into three hierarchical layers: the Physics Perception Layer, the Detection and Attribution Layer, and the Reasoning and Diagnosis Layer.
In the Physics Perception Layer, raw multi-modal sensor inputs—including voltage, current, and temperature—are integrated with domain-specific physics knowledge.
This knowledge formulates mechanism-driven rules, evaluating physical metrics like post-charge thermal states to create an initial numeric-to-semantic bridge.
These rules transform the raw continuous signals into a structured feature matrix for downstream classification.
In the Detection and Attribution Layer, a gradient boosting decision tree processes the feature matrix to classify the operating state as normal or abnormal.
Upon detecting an anomaly, a SHAP explainer attributes the top feature contributions, acting as a secondary bridge to interpret the non-linear decision boundaries.
Both the physical mechanism rules and the SHAP feature attributions are then forwarded to the Reasoning and Diagnosis Layer.
These inputs are integrated into a structured formatting template to dynamically construct the agent prompt.
The prompt is passed into the DeepSeek-R1 Agent Core, which synthesizes the physical and statistical evidence.
Finally, the agent generates a human-readable Diagnosis Report detailing the final diagnosis result, underlying root cause, and actionable maintenance advice.

before.text: The shape generation process begins by sampling Gaussian noise.
This noise is mapped into a latent feature vector.
The feature vector is processed by a primitive prediction network to estimate the parameters of basic geometric building blocks.
These predicted parameters are routed into parallel streams, starting with the cover branch.
Within the cover branch, the framework predicts a set of convex primitives.
It also predicts primitive inverses to represent negative spaces.
These primitives and inverses are grouped together using a differentiable intersection operation to form complex convex parts.
This produces an intermediate intersected shape representation.
A union operation then aggregates these parts, applying dropout to encourage robust feature learning and prevent overfitting.
This yields the final intermediate cover shape, representing the overall base volume of the target object.
Concurrently, the predicted parameters are also routed to the residual branch.
The residual branch similarly predicts convex primitives,
as well as primitive inverses.
These are combined using a differentiable intersection operation,
creating an intermediate intersected residual shape.
A union operation, also utilizing dropout, aggregates these components.
This produces the intermediate residual shape, which captures the detailed cavities and concavities.
To construct the final geometry, a constructive difference operation is applied between the cover shape and the residual shape.
This subtraction yields the reconstructed final shape.
The generated outputs are optimized against the target given shape.
The cover loss computes the deviation between the intermediate cover shape and the given shape to ensure the base volume is accurate.
Simultaneously, the residual loss measures the deviation of the residual shape against the given shape, guiding the network to carve out the correct negative spaces.

Before looking inside, we see that the Cover Branch ultimately outputs an intermediate cover shape, S_C, representing the base volume.
Similarly, the Residual Branch outputs an intermediate residual shape, S_R, capturing detailed cavities.
Now, let's reveal the inner workings. Inside the Cover Branch, the network predicts convex primitives and primitive inverses.
These are combined via a differentiable intersection operation to form an intermediate intersected shape.
A union operation with dropout then aggregates these parts to produce the final cover shape.
Inside the Residual Branch, we similarly predict convex primitives and primitive inverses representing negative spaces.
An intersection operation combines these to form the intermediate intersected residual shape.
A union operation with dropout aggregates these components into the final residual shape.
With both intermediate shapes generated, a constructive difference operation is applied between the cover and residual shapes.
This subtraction yields the reconstructed final shape.
The generated outputs are optimized against the target given shape.
The cover loss computes the deviation between the intermediate cover shape and the given shape to ensure base volume accuracy.
Simultaneously, the residual loss measures the deviation of the residual shape against the given shape to guide negative space carving.

examples.prompt: Remove the branch to the Count Constraint module.

before.text: The processing pipeline begins with the ingestion of raw video frames or static images depicting a crowded scene.
These images are passed directly into the density estimation stage.
Here, a density estimation model maps the spatial distribution of the crowd, generating a continuous density map where high-intensity regions indicate dense clusters of individuals.
The generated density map is then forwarded to the segmentation module.
The density segmentation module processes the map to isolate distinct crowd patches and identify cluster boundaries.
Simultaneously, these segmented regions are analyzed to establish quantitative constraints.
The count constraint mechanism assigns preliminary numerical counts to individual segmented regions, establishing strict quantitative bounds that constrain the subsequent optimization.
Both the segmented regions and the count constraints are then fed into the main optimization block.
Within this block, a sliding region-of-interest window scans the scene to localize potential targets.
The sliding window outputs are then formulated into an integer programming problem.
The integer programming module solves a linear system that matches regional counts with spatial location variables via a transformation matrix.
The optimized spatial variables are then passed to the bounding box estimator.
The bounding box estimation module refines these optimization outputs to determine the precise boundaries of each individual.
These refined coordinates are mapped back onto the original scene to produce the final output.
Finally, the system generates the detection results, marking each individual in the crowd with a precise green bounding box.

after.text: The processing pipeline begins with the ingestion of raw video frames or static images of the targeted scene.
Next, a density estimation model is applied to map the spatial distribution of the crowd, generating a continuous density map where high-intensity regions indicate dense clusters of individuals.

The generated density map is then processed through a density segmentation module to isolate distinct crowd patches and cluster boundaries, while a count constraint mechanism assigns preliminary numerical counts to these regions.
These segmented regions and count constraints are then passed into the optimization block to resolve individual locations.
Within this block, a sliding region-of-interest window scans the scene to evaluate potential localizations.
An integer programming module then solves a linear system, matching regional counts with spatial location variables via a transformation matrix.
Finally, the bounding box estimation module refines these optimization outputs to establish precise spatial boundaries.
This produces the final detection results, marking each individual in the scene with a precise green bounding box.

examples.prompt: Consider a case where the guessed number is 45. Animate the given flowchart accordingly

before.text: The numerical categorization workflow begins at the start node.
The control flow moves to the data ingestion phase.
Here, the system prompts for and captures an unknown quantitative variable, designated as the guess number.
This inputted value is then routed to the primary threshold evaluation.
The system evaluates whether the guess number is less than or equal to ten.
If this condition is true,
the variable is definitively classified as a small number.
If the condition is false, meaning the value strictly exceeds ten, the data is passed to the secondary range assessment.
This compound decision gate checks if the number is greater than ten and less than or equal to eighty.
If this condition evaluates to true,
the workflow categorizes the input as a medium number.
If the condition is false, indicating the value is strictly greater than eighty,

examples.prompt: We consider an scenario where the power light of the computer is ON but the computer is not turning on. Animate the given flowchart accordingly.

before.text: The diagnostic workflow begins with an initial evaluation of the system's state.
First, the protocol checks whether the computer successfully turns on, dividing the evaluation into two primary diagnostic branches.
In the system initialization branch, if the computer successfully turns on, the workflow evaluates whether any error reports have been generated.
If an error report is present, the workflow requires performing a specific search for the provided error message to resolve the conflict.
Alternatively, if no error reports are detected, the device is verified as fully functional, terminating the process with a 'Computer Okay' state.
In the power failure branch, if the computer fails to turn on, the protocol investigates the physical power delivery mechanism by checking the status of the computer's power indicator light.
If the power light is illuminated, the system state is classified as 'PC ON', indicating that power is reaching the unit despite the boot failure.
Conversely, if the power light is not on, indicating a total lack of power delivery, the workflow directs the user to physically check the computer power cord to resolve the disconnection.

Since the power light is illuminated, the system state is classified as 'PC ON', indicating that power is reaching the unit despite the boot failure.

before.text: The computational workflow begins here to calculate the arithmetic mean of a dataset.
First, the system initializes the necessary computational variables to track the running sum and data count.
Next, an input operation is executed to define the total quantity of expected data points, which sets the threshold for the loop.
The control flow then reaches a decision gate to verify if all expected numbers have been entered.
If there are pending data points, the system executes an input operation to capture the most recent sequential value.
This newly acquired value is immediately added to the running sum.
The workflow then loops back to the decision gate to repeat the accumulation cycle.
Once all numbers have been successfully entered, the algorithm breaks the loop and calculates the average by dividing the total sum by the count of data points.
The system then executes a terminal output operation to print the computed average.
Finally, the process concludes and stops.

examples.prompt: Animate only along the branch that starts with the Input video and ends with Image Segmentation

before.text: The pipeline begins with the input video stream, capturing the target object from multiple viewpoints.
These video frames serve as the primary visual source for downstream 2D processing and segmentation.
The input video frames are then routed to the super-pixels module to group homogeneous image regions.
Decomposing the frames into super-pixels simplifies the visual representation and reduces downstream computational complexity.
These super-pixels are passed to the 2D-3D joint segmentation module to establish spatial and appearance consistency.
The joint segmentation module optimizes the boundaries to produce highly accurate 2D image segmentations.
These final image segmentations cleanly isolate the target object from the background across all video frames.

examples.prompt: Consider the Facial Feature Extractor and the Person Dictionary to be part of a single module and animate them accordingly.

before.text: The workflow begins with the Facial Feature Extractor, which is designed to learn a robust representation of facial characteristics.
Training data is first collected to feed into the feature extraction pipeline.
A state-of-the-art convolutional neural network is then trained on this dataset to learn highly discriminative facial features.
Next, the Person Dictionary module builds a reference database of target entities.
It starts by selecting specific entities of interest and gathering exemplary images for them from the web.
The pre-trained convolutional neural network is then applied to extract facial features from these gathered images.
A filtering step is subsequently applied to reduce noise and remove incorrect or low-quality images from the web-based dataset.
In parallel, the system accesses the Internet Archive to retrieve target media content.
The system targets archived web news according to a predefined search space.
This web content contains the raw images in which the target persons will be identified.
The final phase is Person Identification, which processes the archived images to locate and verify the target entities.
First, face detection is performed on the retrieved web content to locate any faces present in the images.
For each detected face, facial features are extracted using the pre-trained convolutional neural network model.
These extracted features are then compared against the filtered Person Dictionary in the face verification step.
Finally, the identified entities and their co-occurrences are visualized to explore relations and media coverage.

after.text: The workflow of the person identification framework begins with training a facial feature extractor and building a person dictionary.
The Facial Feature Extractor block is responsible for learning a robust representation of facial characteristics.
It utilizes a training dataset containing facial images.
This dataset is used to train a convolutional neural network, or CNN. The CNN learns to extract robust feature representations to describe facial characteristics.
Next, the Person Dictionary block defines a lexicon of target entities for a given domain.
First, entities are selected, and exemplary images are gathered from the web using an image search engine.
The trained CNN is then applied to extract facial features from these gathered images.
A filtering step is performed to reduce noise and improve the quality of the sample dataset.
To identify these entities in real-world data, the system retrieves content from the Internet Archive.
The Internet Archive serves as the primary source of historical web data.
Web content, such as images from archived web pages, is extracted according to a predefined search space.
These web pages contain the target images in which persons of interest will be identified.
Finally, the Person Identification block processes the retrieved web images to locate and verify the target entities.
First, face detection is performed on the web images to locate any faces.
For each detected face, features are extracted using the trained CNN model.
Face verification is then conducted by comparing the extracted features against the filtered Person Dictionary.
Finally, the identified occurrences and relations of the persons of interest are visualized for analysis.
